title: Verified Evidence Must Govern Vietnam’s Dog-Trade Reform
excerpt: A trade defense cannot replace records, quarantine, or public accountability. Vietnam needs verified evidence, stronger enforcement, and abolition by 2030.
body_html:
When a family dog disappears, grief is immediate. When authorities cannot publicly trace where animals came from, how they moved, or whether they passed veterinary controls, accountability disappears too. No verified case, court record, seizure report, or government dataset accompanies claims supplied for this dispatch. Those gaps do not prove every animal was stolen or every seller broke law. They prove public scrutiny cannot stop at slogans.

Tradition cannot answer a missing paper trail

“Tradition” does not establish lawful origin. “Farm-raised” does not establish a farm. Any commercial claim needs traceable records: source, owner or operator, transport route, veterinary inspection, quarantine status, slaughter location, and food-safety oversight. Without those records, consumers and communities cannot distinguish lawful activity from theft, illegal transport, or regulatory breach.

Public health needs facts, not reassurance

Rabies spreads when infected saliva enters through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. Handling sick animals, uninspected slaughter, and bite attacks create separate risks. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. See World Health Organization rabies guidance.

Vietnamese communities deserve transparent protection

Families, pet owners, veterinarians, and local authorities can demand records, report suspected theft, insist on quarantine enforcement, and reject unsupported trade defenses. Household rabies exposure and commercial supply chains are parallel biosecurity concerns, not automatically one proven chain.

SDE’s demand goes beyond official public-health targets: complete abolition of the dog-meat trade by 2030. Add your name to that public demand. Sign the national petition and follow campaign updates reaching decision-makers.

Claims about “tradition” or “farm-raised dogs” cannot answer those questions without records. No verified court record, seizure report, government dataset, or named incident supplied for this dispatch proves that every animal in Vietnam’s trade was stolen or that commercial meat directly caused a particular rabies case. Precision matters. So does accountability.

Rabies spreads when infected saliva enters bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, then seek urgent medical assessment for vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal.

Vietnamese families, pet owners, veterinarians, and local leaders deserve traceable supply chains, enforced quarantine, and protection from theft and cruelty. SDE calls for complete abolition by 2030.
